opus-5.5.text:
I think the big one is the assumption that because the end-to-end model wins, it must have discovered something fundamentally different from the structure we were trying to impose, or that it isn't using structure at all. Those are two separate claims, and the benchmark number alone doesn't support either.

When you look inside these models, you often find that they've learned representations that line up surprisingly well with the structured abstractions we built by hand. That might be something like compositional meaning representations, or something that behaves like a parse, or something that tracks the state of the world. So the right conclusion often isn't "structure doesn't matter." It's closer to "structure matters, and the model can learn it from data more flexibly than we could specify it." The win may come from the model handling the messy cases at the edges, the parts our hand-designed formalism couldn't capture, while still relying on something close to the formalism for the core of the problem.

The opposite mistake is also worth watching for. Researchers sometimes assume the model is solving the task the way we would. Then it turns out it's exploiting dataset artifacts or shallow correlations that happen to work well on the test distribution. Outperforming a structured model on a benchmark tells you about that benchmark. It doesn't tell you the model has the systematic generalization the structured model was designed to guarantee.

So my advice is to treat the comparison as the start of an investigation, not the conclusion. Probe the representations. Test on out-of-distribution and compositional splits. Ask which parts of the structure the model has recovered and which parts it has discarded. Very often the interesting scientific answer is in that gap, and it can tell you something about the problem itself, not just about which architecture is better.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that outperforming a structured model does not show the end-to-end model solves the task the same way, and may instead reflect dataset artifacts or shallow correlations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the one I'd flag most is the assumption that because the end-to-end model does better on the benchmark, it must have discovered a better representation of the problem than the one we would have written down by hand. And that's a very tempting inference, because the structured model encodes a hypothesis about how the task decomposes — these are the latent variables, these are the compositional pieces — and when the neural model beats it, it's natural to conclude the hypothesis was wrong, or at least unnecessary.

But there are a lot of other things that can be going on. The neural model might be winning because it's exploiting regularities in the dataset that have nothing to do with the structure we care about. It might be winning because the structured model was just undertrained or badly parameterized, and the comparison isn't really structure versus no structure, it's a good optimizer versus a bad one. Or, and this is the case I find most interesting, the neural model might actually have learned something that looks a lot like the structure we hypothesized — it's just that it's distributed across a bunch of hidden units and we can't see it by looking at the architecture.

So the thing to be wary of is treating the architecture as evidence about the solution. The architecture tells you what the model is capable of representing, not what it ended up representing. If you want to know whether the structure is really there, you have to go look — probe the representations, test on inputs that require compositional generalization, see whether the behavior breaks in the places where a structured model would also break. And in a lot of cases when people have done that, the answer is messier than either "structure is unnecessary" or "it secretly learned the grammar." It's usually some of both, and the interesting question is which parts.

r001.rationale: The response warns that outperforming a structured model does not show the end-to-end model has the same or a better task representation, and says its architecture alone does not reveal what it learned.

astra-6.text: I think you have to be careful about assuming that because an end-to-end model outperforms a model with some explicit structure, that structure must be unnecessary—or that the end-to-end model isn’t using it. It might be learning something very much like the structure you built into the other model, but learning a better version of it, or using it more flexibly. There are also differences in optimization and how you allocate model capacity. So the performance comparison tells you which implementation works better, but it doesn’t, by itself, tell you what computation is responsible. To get at that, you need experiments that distinguish those possibilities.

r001.rationale: The response says better performance alone does not reveal what computation the end-to-end model uses, and it may be learning something like the structured model’s structure.

sol-6.1.text: I think we should be wary of assuming that the end-to-end model’s success means the structure was unnecessary. You might compare a model with an explicit parsing step to one that goes directly from input to output, and find that the latter works better. But that doesn’t tell you whether it has learned to do something like parsing internally. It might have learned a better representation of that structure, or one that’s better suited to the task. So there’s a distinction between saying we don’t need to explicitly supervise or hard-code a particular intermediate representation and saying that the underlying computation doesn’t need that representation at all.

r001.rationale: It warns that an end-to-end model’s better performance does not show the structured computation is unnecessary, since the model may have learned that structure internally.
